extracted.intended_audience: NIH study section members, grant reviewers and chairs, research administrators and scholars of peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and guidance about social-interactional factors (e.g., score calibration talk, laughter, chair behavior) that influence reviewers' priority score changes during NIH study section meetings. Useful for people running or participating in grant peer review panels to understand and reduce social bias in scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score Calibration Talk (SCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discourse practice where a study section member discusses and interprets the scoring rather than the content of a grant application (termed 'score calibration talk' or SCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCT is the high-level category of interaction the paper examines; it can influence scoring outcomes. The study identifies SCT as distinct from content discussion and recommends awareness of SCT during review meetings because it can change reviewers' scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-initiated SCT
rubrics_metrics.description: When a panelist provides commentary about their own scoring (example: 'So I gave it a four, which was probably generous').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper found that self-initiated SCT alone was not associated with immediate score change when shared laughter did not ensue (no cases of immediate score change when a panelist initiated SCT but no shared laughter). Treat self-initiated SCT as less likely, by itself, to induce score changes but still monitor for downstream social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other-initiated SCT
rubrics_metrics.description: When a panelist challenges the scoring of an assigned reviewer (example: 'Yeah, that was generous.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only other-initiated SCT correlated with changes from the initial to the final score among the assigned reviewers of R01 applications. Monitor and limit challenges that focus on scoring rather than on application content, because such challenges are more likely to precipitate score changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared laughter during SCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of shared laughter among study section members that occur during SCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared laughter significantly increased the likelihood of immediate score change (OR = 16; 95% CI: 1.09–234.25, p = .04). While laughter can serve pro-social functions, the authors recommend refraining from shared laughter during SCT because it can introduce interpersonal pressure that alters the range of scoring. Chairs and participants should be attentive to laughter's potential biasing effect during scoring discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair-initiated SCT
rubrics_metrics.description: SCT initiated by the chair of the study section rather than by a regular panelist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chair initiation of SCT was highly associated with score change (OR = 36; 95% CI: 1.77–731.56, p = .02). Because the chair has status and influence, the paper advises chairs to be cautious when initiating SCT and to check that their influence does not precipitate score changes; chairs should avoid exerting implicit pressure on reviewers' scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring of individual scores to declared reviewer scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual panelists' scores are anchored to the scores declared publicly by the assigned reviewers (usually three), and the final priority score is an average of each panelist’s score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individual scores are publicly declared and others' declared scores serve as anchors, anchoring effects can propagate through the panel. Review processes should recognize this procedural feature as a source of potential bias and consider practices to mitigate anchoring (e.g., structured discussion protocols, private re-scoring procedures) to preserve reasoned scoring focused on application content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to minimize social-pressure influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance arising from the findings: chairs and reviewers should be alerted to SCT and its potential consequences, chairs should be cautious when initiating SCT, and participants should refrain from laughter during SCT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly recommend that chairs check their influence and avoid initiating SCT that could bias scores, and that laughter be refrained from during SCT where reasoned scoring is the explicit goal. These procedural recommendations function as operational standards for conducting fair grant review meetings.
